evidence.field: evolution records; oracle-bone entry 合集822正, bronze entry 集成04025, seal-script entry 說文; interpretation
evidence.text: The page catalogs 身 forms under oracle bone (including 合集822正), bronze (集成04025), Chu manuscripts, and small seal script. It interprets the old graph as a woman with a large pregnant abdomen. This supports the existence and broad evolution of early forms, but the page’s brief interpretation does not date individual forms or establish that pregnancy, rather than abdomen, was the graph’s first meaning.
evidence.title: 漢字「身」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 / Multi-function Chinese Character Database, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 形義通解; oracle-bone and bronze evidence; dated textual examples
evidence.text: The database analyzes the oracle-bone and bronze graph as 人 with the abdomen marked, possibly with a navel dot; it proposes abdomen as the original meaning. It cites an oracle-bone use in 合集822正 for the king’s abdominal illness. It separately cites bronze uses for person/body, protection of the king’s person, one’s own action, and a person’s lifetime or era. For Warring States manuscript evidence, it cites Guodian Laozi B strip 8 for 身 meaning body and Qinghua manuscript 程寤 strip 9 for the body. It traces “pregnancy” to the phrase 有身 in the Odes, 大雅·大明, and later whole-body and self meanings. These are the database’s semantic analysis and source citations; the page does not provide absolute dates for each inscription or manuscript.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 身

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Character Structure Database
evidence.field: graphic chronology and graph interpretation
evidence.text: Its account differs in emphasis from CUHK’s: it describes the early form as a pregnant woman with a large abdomen. CUHK instead identifies the marked area as abdomen and treats pregnancy as a semantic development. The early image is compatible with both descriptions; the inspected pages do not demonstrate that the image itself distinguishes a pregnant figure from an abdomen-marked person.
evidence.title: 漢字「身」：字形演變

evidence.source: 《說文解字》 entry as reproduced by CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 《說文》 explanation
evidence.text: The reproduced text says 身 means 躳 (body/person oneself), depicts a person’s body, and is formed from 人 with 𠂆 as phonetic. This is Xu Shen’s historical account, not independent confirmation of the graph’s original structure. The inspected paleographic database interpretation instead treats the early graph as a marked abdomen; no reviewed source established 𠂆 as the phonetic in the earliest graph.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 身

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, 2015 draft discussing Old Chinese and excavated texts
evidence.field: section 4.1; 身 and 仁 phonetic use and reconstruction
evidence.text: The authors state that examples in pre-Qin documents write 仁 rén ‘kind’ with 身 shēn as phonetic. They use this evidence to reconstruct 仁 *niŋ and 身 *n̥i[ŋ], with Middle Chinese nyin and syin respectively. This is evidence for a phonetic role in the compound/graph 仁 and a reconstruction argument; it is not a claim that 身 itself is a whole-graph loan for a pronoun. The draft’s prose does not identify a particular manuscript or provide a date for the examples in the inspected passage.

gaps: No manuscript-level citation or absolute date for the particular excavated 仁 written with 身 as phonetic was recoverable from the inspected passage; the phonetic role and reconstruction are asserted by Baxter and Sagart, while its individual exemplar remains unspecified here.

The two paleographic interpretations—pregnant woman versus person with marked abdomen—remain a genuine difference in explanatory emphasis. The consulted references do not establish which visual interpretation is decisive.

The broad script sequence includes oracle bone, bronze, Chu manuscript and small-seal forms, but the pages inspected do not establish a complete dated lineage or identify any specific graphic corruption/transformation between forms.
No independently established early borrowing of 身 for a pronoun was found. CUHK describes later self/reflexive senses as semantic extensions; do not label these a phonetic loan on this evidence.

Exact Unicode character-specific Unihan pages for 身 and 仁 were unavailable to the web tool; supplied local 身 row was checked, but the required clickable upstream record could not be verified. No local 仁 reading row was supplied.
The upstream Baxter–Sagart 2014 PDF search result was found but returned 502 when opened. Local 身 notation was preserved exactly; direct 2015 draft corroboration exists.

The early-graph interpretations remain disputed: Academia Sinica describes a pregnant woman, while CUHK analyzes a person with the abdomen marked and proposes abdomen as the original sense. The reviewed sources do not establish a visually decisive interpretation.
The references give inscription and manuscript identifiers but not absolute dates for every use; no continuous dated graphic lineage or specific corruption sequence was established.

The proposed later semantic steps (abdomen to pregnancy/body to whole person/self) are CUHK's analysis. Individual cited examples support uses, but do not independently prove every semantic transition.
The Shuowen component statement 人 plus 𠂆 as phonetic is a historical account; no reviewed source establishes 𠂆 as a phonetic in the earliest graph.

Exact Unicode Unihan character-specific records for 身 and 申 were inaccessible. The exact supplied local row for 身 is preserved as local data; no 申 sound-component analysis was needed for the supported graph history.

The 2014 Baxter–Sagart table PDF was found but could not be opened. Its supplied local row is not presented as directly inspected upstream material; the accessible 2015 draft uses a different visible OC notation for 身 and supports the phonetic evidence from 身 in 仁.
A whole-graph loan of 身 for a pronoun was not established. CUHK describes self/reflexive meanings as semantic extensions; this research does not classify them as borrowing.

The Commons oracle and seal files are modern vector redrawings rather than artifact photographs. The seal example clarifies a later script form but is not evidence for the disputed earliest interpretation.
